repairs.before:
Compare experimentally obtained isotherms for a real gas (Figure 55) to see how the liquid-vapor coexistence segment changes near the critical point.
We compare the same pure substance and the same total mass at different constant temperatures.
We are not assuming that all substances at all temperatures follow one curve.
repairs.after:
An isotherm shows how pressure changes with volume while temperature stays fixed.
Figure 55 compares curves for the same pure substance and the same total mass.
Below the critical temperature, each curve has a flat part where liquid and vapor are both present.
These flat parts become shorter at higher temperatures below the critical temperature.
We are not assuming that all substances at all temperatures follow one curve.

repairs.before:
The textbook's statements about a maximum liquid volume and maximum saturated vapor pressure refer to endpoints of the coexistence curves discussed here.
They mean the endpoint approached by a fixed mass of saturated liquid and the critical endpoint of the saturated vapor pressure curve.
They do not mean that every liquid has a condition-independent maximum volume, or that a substance's pressure cannot exceed its critical pressure.
repairs.after:
The textbook's statements about a maximum liquid volume and maximum saturated vapor pressure concern the coexistence curves discussed here.
For a fixed mass, the saturated-liquid branch ends at the critical volume.
The saturated vapor pressure curve ends at the critical pressure.

These are not limits for every possible state.
Pressure can exceed the critical pressure, and liquid volume depends on the conditions.

repairs.before:
Further compression produces a denser single-phase fluid with liquid-like properties.
We should not unconditionally call it a cylinder full of ordinary liquid.
This path has no finite interval of liquid-vapor coexistence like the one below the critical temperature.

There is no interface separating two phases.
The continuous transition here concerns phase state and density.
It does not mean that physical properties near the critical point show no marked changes.
repairs.after:
Further compression makes the single-phase fluid denser and more liquid-like.
It does not split into separate liquid and vapor regions.
Unlike the curve below the critical temperature, this curve has no flat coexistence segment covering a range of volumes.

There is no interface separating two phases.
Density changes continuously along this path, though other physical properties can still change strongly near the critical point.
